content.title: Where the knobs start
content.text: Training begins with random knobs. Rewind the digit network to that start: its loss over the 3,823 pictures is 2.2916, and the knob of pill 04 happens to sit at 0.37. Pill 07 drew bowls, but drawing one costs 121 full passes over every picture, and there are 2,778 knobs. Training cannot afford to look. All it has is where it stands: one knob value, one loss. The question of this pill: from that alone, which way is downhill, and how steep?

content.title: Nudge it and measure
content.text: Turn the knob up by 1 and measure again: the loss is 2.2775, down by 0.01411. Divide the change in loss by the change in the knob: −0.01411 per unit of knob. That is a slope, the same rise over run as m in pill 05. Its sign gives the direction: negative means the loss falls as the knob grows, so downhill is to the right. Its size says how steep the ground is: here, gentle. Two measurements, one division, and the dark has a direction in it.

content.title: Shrink the nudge
content.text: A nudge of 1 measures the average over a whole stretch, and the curve may bend inside it. Shrink the nudge: 0.1 gives −0.01937, 0.01 gives −0.01986, 0.001 gives −0.01990. The ratios settle on one number, −0.01991: the slope at this exact point, the ground under the feet rather than the ground a step away. In maths this number is the derivative of the loss with respect to the knob, and training uses nothing else. The recipe is plain: nudge, measure, divide, and shrink the nudge until the answer stops moving.

content.title: The curve nobody drew
content.text: Now draw the whole curve as a check, the one training never sees. At the knob’s point a straight line with slope −0.0199 hugs the curve: right there the two are indistinguishable. Elsewhere the slope is different: steep down at −4, −0.0537, steep up at 5, +0.0560. At the bottom, w = 1.92, the slope is 0.0000: flat ground. That is how a bottom is recognised without seeing the bowl: every slope is zero. And a slope is local. It describes the ground at one point and promises nothing about how far the bottom is, which is why pill 07 ended on small turns.

content.title: The slope of a weight is its input
content.text: Pills 05 and 06 promised one slope for free. Take neuron 10 of the first row reading the 7, and its weight on pixel 21, 0.485. Turn that weight by 1 and the neuron’s sum z moves by 0.625, the brightness of that pixel. Turn it by 0.1 and z moves by 0.0625. The ratio is 0.625 every time, at every point, because z against one weight is a straight line, and a line has one slope: the input on that wire. No nudging needed. A dark pixel gives a flat line: its weight can move all it likes and z does not change, slope 0. Pixels 0 and 39 are dark in all 3,823 pictures, so the 64 knobs reading them have slope exactly 0 for the whole set. They can never learn anything.

content.title: One slope per knob
content.text: Every knob has a slope at the point where the network stands: 2,778 of them. At the random start, teal where the loss falls when the knob grows, pink where it rises, brighter where steeper. The steepest is a wire into the score for 7, −0.0472; 1,374 knobs want up, 1,340 want down, 64 are exactly flat, the dark pixels. After training the same field is about five times fainter, 0.00112 on average against 0.00599, but not zero: training stopped after 60 passes, near a bottom, not on it. That is the little leftover downhill of pill 07. One problem remains. Measuring by nudging costs one pass over 3,823 pictures per knob, 10.6 million picture readings for a single small turn, and training takes thousands of turns. The next pill gets all 2,778 slopes from one pass.
